A leadership purpose is a short account of why you lead and for whom. Minnesota Management and Budget's Competency Definition Guide places Leading Self first among the State's five leader competencies and defines it as a commitment to personal and professional growth through self-reflection and self-improvement. Its key skills include self-awareness, integrity, identity and cultural humility. The Guide also speaks of a State leader in any capacity, such as the head of a team, a committee or a partnership, so a purpose is worth writing whether or not you supervise anyone.

Most first drafts of a purpose describe the work rather than the people. Phrases such as delivering quality results or supporting my team are true, but they could describe any job anywhere. They also leave a question open: quality for whom, judged by whom? The Guide says State leaders are accountable to all Minnesotans. In human services that includes people who receive services and their families, providers, county and lead agency partners, colleagues, and members of the public who may never contact the agency but depend on it.

A useful purpose names who it is for and what should be different for them. Start by listing the groups your work touches. Then ask whose experience you hear about most and whose you rarely hear at all. A licensing lead may hear often from providers and seldom from people living in licensed settings. A policy lead may hear from counties and seldom from the family members who complete the paperwork. Write one sentence that names a group you serve and the change you want them to notice, then a second about the colleagues you lead or work beside.

Your purpose is a personal guide, not a job requirement. It does not change your position description, your performance expectations or the agency's mission, and no one will collect or review it. Formal duties come from your position description, your supervisor and Human Resources. The department's Equity Policy commits it to operating as a multicultural and intercultural organization, and a purpose that names who you serve is one way to carry that commitment into your own daily decisions.

changes.before:
Everyone carries a picture of what a good leader looks like. It forms early, from family, school, faith communities, first jobs and the bosses we admired or avoided. In many workplaces the picture is confident, quick to speak, decisive and visible. Those are real strengths. They are also cultural preferences. Other traditions, and many people within any one tradition, value leaders who consult widely, speak last, build agreement or lead through steady service rather than presence.

A default picture shapes decisions without being noticed. It shows up in who we describe as having potential, whose ideas we treat as strong and who gets asked to present. Shore and Chung's 2021 review of inclusive leadership describes an assimilation pattern, in which a leader treats everyone the same and people belong only if they fit the established way. The authors note that the evidence is still at an early stage, but the pattern is easy to recognize: one style becomes the measure, and people who lead differently are read as less ready.

The intercultural development continuum, published by IDI, LLC, can describe how habits of recognizing leadership change. A Minimization habit sounds like: good leadership is the same everywhere, so I look for confidence and initiative. Minnesota Management and Budget's Guide lists a similar in-progress behavior, recognizing cultural differences but overemphasizing commonalities. An Acceptance habit notices that speaking first and speaking last can both be leadership. An Adaptation habit changes the routine: asking for written input before a meeting, crediting whoever built agreement, and naming results and relationships when you recognize leadership.

Examining your own picture is ordinary leadership work, not a confession. Ask whose interests your idea of a good leader serves, which colleagues it helps you see and whom it might cause you to miss. Then test it against the work: which ways of leading actually produce good outcomes for the people your team serves? Where your picture could touch formal decisions such as hiring, selection or acting assignments, those belong with Human Resources and their set criteria; your part is to notice your default and keep it out of the way.

Values guide leadership only when they show up in what you do. Fairness, respect and transparency are common values, and almost no one argues against them. Their weakness is that they are hard to see. Washington State's enterprise leadership competencies, for example, begin with modeling and championing the organization's culture and values, which treats values as something a leader shows in practice rather than simply holds.

An observable commitment turns a value into a habit someone else could see. Fairness might become: I explain how I divide work and invite questions about it. Respect might become: when a decision affects people who receive services, I hear from some of them before it is final. Transparency might become: I tell people what I do not yet know. Write each one so that a colleague watching a week of your work could tell whether you kept it. Keep it to two or three. More is hard to remember on a busy day, and a short list is easier to share with someone who can tell you when you slip.

Pressure is where commitments are tested. Deloitte's 2016 report on the six signature traits of inclusive leadership notes that time pressure and fatigue raise the risk that bias shapes a decision. Values come under the same strain: under a deadline, the quickest route usually runs through familiar people and habits. Learn your warning signs, such as skipping a step because it is only this once. Then plan the smallest adaptation that keeps the commitment, such as a short accessible summary and one focused question, and check afterward whether it reached the people it was meant for.

Some tensions are yours to resolve and some are not. If a deadline squeezes your own practice, you can adapt it and be honest about the tradeoff. If you believe a directive conflicts with a legal requirement, raise it with the responsible program area or legal counsel rather than deciding alone. Concerns about discrimination go to the equal opportunity office, and questions about workload or assignments under a labor agreement go to Human Resources or labor relations. A commitment gives you no authority you do not already have; it tells you when to speak up.

Values guide leadership only when they show up in what you do. Values such as fairness, respect and transparency need practical meaning in a particular situation. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader guide includes alignment between stated values and purpose among proficient behaviors for Leading Others. A commitment describes how you intend to put a value into practice.

An observable commitment turns a value into a habit someone else could see. Fairness might become: I explain how I divide work and invite questions about it. Respect might become: when a decision affects people who receive services, I use appropriate, accessible ways to seek their input while the relevant choices remain open. Transparency might become: I tell people what I do not yet know. Write each one so that a colleague watching a week of your work could tell whether you kept it. Keep it to two or three. More is hard to remember on a busy day, and a short list is easier to share with someone who can tell you when you slip.

A short purpose statement is easier to use than a long one. Two or three sentences are enough: one about who your leadership is for and what should change for them, one about the colleagues you lead or work beside, and one commitment that shows the purpose in action. One example: I lead so that people who use our services get answers they can act on, and so that colleagues newer to the work get real chances to grow. Write it in your own words, as you would say it to a colleague. If it would sound strange out loud, it will be hard to recall when a decision comes.

Other people can see what you cannot. Minnesota Management and Budget's Guide describes a proficient leader as one who seeks feedback, listens and modifies their approach, and its expert level includes admitting they are not always right. Shore and Chung suggest that one first step toward inclusive leadership is for leaders to ask for feedback on their own inclusiveness. Choose one person you trust who sees you work. Someone whose background or role differs from yours may notice defaults you have never had reason to question. Share your statement and ask one question: where do you see this in how I lead, and where do you not? Listen, thank them and resist explaining.

A purpose is tested by a real decision. After a decision that mattered, such as how work was divided, which partners were consulted or how a change was explained, reread your statement. Ask what happened, for whom, and whether the people your purpose names would recognize it in what you did. Then sort what you learned into what you will keep, what you will change and what you will stop. A gap between the statement and the decision is information, not failure.

Your statement is private unless you choose to share it. It is not a performance goal, and no one will collect, rate or record it. Keep notes about your own practice, not about the people who gave you feedback or were affected by the decision. If reviewing a decision raises a question about pay, classification, discipline or work assignments under a labor agreement, take it to Human Resources or labor relations instead of working it out alone. How you divide ordinary work and explain it is yours to improve. Return to your statement every few months, or after any decision that tested it.
